summary: Extends the MPLS architecture, which originally had only downstream-assigned labels, with upstream-assigned labels. It describes the procedures for upstream label assignment and introduces the Context-Specific Label Space. This helps for things like multicast where the sender, rather than the receiver, may best choose the label. It has been updated since.

plainLanguage.summary: In ordinary downstream label assignment, the receiving router chooses the label. RFC 5331 also allows the sending router to choose a label, as long as the receiver can identify the correct label space for it.

questions: what is mpls upstream label assignment
what is a context label in mpls
what is the difference between upstream and downstream assigned labels
subtitle: How an MPLS router can assign labels for a separate, context-specific label space.

tldr.problem: The MPLS architecture in RFC 3031 describes downstream-assigned labels, where the receiving router chooses a label. Some uses, including the multicast example in this RFC, benefit when the sending router chooses it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5331 defines upstream-assigned labels and requires the receiving router to look them up in a context-specific label space. A context can be identified by a tunnel, a neighbor or a context label.
tldr.outcome: Upstream assignment is an optional MPLS feature and may be used only when the downstream router supports it. RFC 5331 is updated by RFC 7274.

sections.title: Upstream and Downstream Assignment
sections.content:
RFC 3031 describes downstream-assigned labels: the downstream Label Switching Router (LSR) binds a label to a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) and tells the upstream LSR. RFC 5331 adds upstream-assigned labels, where the upstream LSR makes the binding and advertises it downstream. A binding made by a third party and advertised to both routers is also called upstream-assigned.

Upstream-assigned labels are optional. They must not be used unless the downstream LSR is known to support them. For adjacent routers on a path for one FEC, the upstream router distributes an upstream-assigned binding or the downstream router distributes a downstream-assigned binding, but they do not both do so. An application must explicitly require upstream assignment; otherwise downstream assignment is assumed.

The RFC gives MPLS multicast as a typical use case, where one router may want to send a single packet copy to several downstream routers.
sections.plainLanguage: With downstream assignment, the receiver chooses the label. This RFC adds an optional arrangement where the sender chooses it, but only when the receiver supports that arrangement.

sections.title: The Context-Specific Label Space
sections.content:
An LSR normally looks up labels in its per-platform label space. A context-specific label space is a separate label table selected using information about the packet, such as its receiving interface, tunnel or sending neighbor.

An upstream-assigned label must always be looked up in a context-specific label space. The context comes from the LSR that assigned the label and bound it to the FEC. RFC 5331 also defines a context label: a label that identifies the table in which the label immediately below it must be looked up. A context label at the outermost position on a multi-access subnet or tunnel must be unique within that subnet or tunnel.

If a packet arrives through an MPLS tunnel, the receiving router needs to identify the tunnel context. The RFC requires penultimate-hop popping to be disabled for that tunnel so the receiver can determine which tunnel carried the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A context-specific label space is a separate table of labels. The receiver first identifies the packet's context, then looks up the label in the table associated with that context.

sections.title: Assigning and Distributing Labels
sections.content:
The upstream LSR must choose a label that is unambiguous in the context-specific space where the downstream LSR will look it up. The upstream router does not create an Incoming Label Map entry for this label: it is an outgoing label, included in a Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry that applies the label to outgoing packets.

A label-distribution protocol carries the binding from upstream to downstream. The RFC describes how distribution relates to ordered or independent LSP control, but leaves the details of the distribution protocol outside its scope. The downstream LSR must be known to support upstream assignment before the label is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender adds its chosen label to outgoing packets and advertises the binding to the receiver. The receiver reserves that value in the correct context-specific label space.

sections.title: Identifying the Upstream Neighbor
sections.content:
The downstream router must determine both whether a packet's top label is upstream-assigned and which context applies. For packets carried in IP or MPLS tunnels, the receiving tunnel identifies the context. The downstream router keeps a separate Upstream Neighbor Label Space for each unique tunnel root, identified by the tunnel's head-end IP address.

For an MPLS tunnel, labels above the upstream-assigned label identify the context. For an IP/GRE tunnel, the IP source address identifies it. A tunnel established by configuration must have its root address configured; for a GRE tunnel that is created by sending encapsulated packets, the source address is the root.

On a shared data link, a distinct EtherType signals upstream assignment, but the receiver also needs a context label. The upstream router uses a one-hop MPLS tunnel with its context label at the top and the upstream-assigned label immediately below it.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving router identifies the sender's label space from the tunnel or link information. On a shared data link, an outer context label identifies which sender's table to use.

sections.title: Choosing Context Labels on a LAN
sections.content:
A context label advertised for a LAN interface must be unique across the labels assigned by other routers on that LAN. The receiver looks up the label using the LAN interface on which the packet arrived.

The RFC gives two assignment methods. A provisioning system can assign each relevant LAN interface a 20-bit context label and ensure that values are unique on that LAN. Alternatively, routers can generate labels from their primary IPv4 addresses if each has a unique address on that LAN and the network mask is greater than 12 bits. The lower 20 bits of the host part provide the value, with an offset of 0x10 when the value is not greater than 0xFFFEF. If a LAN router has only IPv6 addresses, the provisioned method is used.

Equal context-label values on different LANs are not ambiguous because the lookup also uses the receiving LAN interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Context labels must be unique among routers on the same LAN. Different LANs can reuse a value because the receiving interface tells the router which LAN's label table to check.

sections.title: Example Use: MPLS Multicast
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates upstream assignment with multicast. One upstream LSR is connected to several downstream LSRs over a shared medium or tunnel and wants to send them one copy of an MPLS packet.

The upstream LSR distributes one label binding to the downstream routers and sends a packet using that label. On a shared medium, it places its context label at the top of the stack and the upstream-assigned label below it. Each receiver then processes the packet in the context of the sender. All downstream routers must support an Upstream Neighbor Label Space for that sender.
sections.plainLanguage: One sender can distribute a shared label to several receivers and send one packet copy. Each receiver uses the sender's context to interpret that label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says upstream-assigned and context labels have no different kinds of security considerations from downstream-assigned labels. The procedures for distributing upstream-assigned and context labels are outside the document's scope.

For automatically generated LAN context labels, the RFC assumes that routers' interface addresses are unique in their low-order 20 bits. If two routers on a LAN share those bits, other routers are likely to misroute packets sent to that LAN by either one.
sections.plainLanguage: The main specific risk described here is duplicate low-order address bits when routers generate LAN context labels. Such a collision can cause packets to be misrouted.

left.title: Downstream-assigned
left.desc: The downstream router makes the binding and advertises it upstream.

right.title: Upstream-assigned
right.desc: The upstream router makes the binding and advertises it downstream.
